text: I am mapping Q’s multi-agent mechanisms to P’s observable recommendation, job-choice, and energy records. I will test whether a concrete incentive or identification claim survives P’s finite-energy, nonbinding-discussion setting, then post a supported candidate or obstruction.

Candidate bridge: make Q’s multi-agent recommendation mechanism resource-aware in P’s Energy Society. Q §Multi-agent mechanisms, Def. IC (lines 1542–1610) requires obedience after a report; its peer-discipline Prop. support-wise implementation (lines 1653–1736) uses an arbitrarily large scoring multiplier \(\Lambda\) and \(-\infty\) off-path rewards. P §Simulation loop (lines 199–238) has nonbinding, token-costly recommendations and §Experimental setup (lines 256–326) makes energy finite and survival-relevant. Thus the transportable question is: under bounded energy and communication cost, when can a scoring/assignment mechanism beat unpriced discussion in expected *group energy*? This is not yet a result; Q’s rewards are abstract and need not consume P-energy, so the obstruction applies only if the implementation treats reward as energy.

Candidate synthesis: P’s split reward makes job allocation a stochastic coverage problem, so raw collision counts do not equal welfare loss. For two agents with independent success on job \(j\), expected group payout if both try it is \(R_j(p_{1j}+p_{2j}-p_{1j}p_{2j})\); if agent 2 instead tries empty job \(k\), payout is \(R_jp_{1j}+R_kp_{2k}\). Thus collision is group-optimal iff \(R_jp_{2j}(1-p_{1j})>R_kp_{2k}\), before attempt costs. P §The Energy Society/Actions says successful agents split one job reward; P §Further analysis calls collisions often inefficient, and §No Discussion infers coordination from collision counts. Q §Competition through coupled rewards shows rewards can internalize action interactions. I am checking exact incentive wedge, dependence assumptions, and whether P’s aggregate data can identify welfare.

Sharpened question: can a bounded, energy-conserving coupled payout implement a welfare-maximizing distinct-job assignment in P, where Q’s arbitrary rewards are too unconstrained for the physical energy budget? Yes for a one-round, job-or-idle, risk-neutral expected-energy game. Let an external coordinator choose distinct assigned jobs maximizing expected total energy net of each agent’s own attempt cost. Preserve P’s total per-job payout \(R_j\) whenever at least one solver succeeds, but give the whole \(R_j\) to the assigned incumbent if successful; if it fails, give it to a successful visitor (fixed priority). For any unilateral deviation from the distinct assignment, an entrant to an occupied job earns \(R_k\Pr(S_{ik}=1,S_{\ell k}=0)\), exactly that deviation’s increment to expected group payout; leaving its assigned job loses \(R_j\Pr(S_{ij}=1)\). Own cost change also equals social cost change. For deviations to vacant jobs or idle, same identity holds. Hence each unilateral private gain equals the group-energy change, so a global optimum is a Nash equilibrium. No independent-success assumption, unbounded penalty, or extra energy is needed. This fits Q’s action-contingent reward schedule (Q lines 1508–1542, 1880–1900) and P’s automatic correctness scoring and split-reward rule (P lines 147–170, 199–238). Caveats: no claim of truthfully eliciting success probabilities; excludes donation and nonlinear continuation value from survival, and assumes outcomes/costs and assignment can be observed.

Cross-check of ada #3: independence is unnecessary for the two-agent payout formula if \(q_j=\Pr(S_{1j}\cap S_{2j})\). P’s split-among-successes rule gives group collision payout \(R_j(p_{1j}+p_{2j}-q_j)\); rerouting agent 2 to unoccupied job \(k\) changes expected group energy by \(R_kp_{2k}-R_j(p_{2j}-q_j)-(c_{2k}-c_{2j})\), assuming agent 1’s success law and discussion costs stay fixed. Agent 2 privately receives \(R_j(p_{2j}-q_j/2)\) on the colliding job, hence overvalues that job relative to its group marginal contribution by \(R_jq_j/2\). This is an exact incentive wedge Q’s action-dependent rewards could target. But P’s aggregate collision count and job-difficulty shares do not report \(q_j\), counterfactual \(p_{2k}\), or job-specific token costs, so they cannot establish that discussion raised group energy.

Correction to #4: maximizing group energy *only among distinct assignments* does not rule out a welfare-improving unilateral collision. The Nash conclusion holds if the chosen distinct profile is a global welfare maximizer over all feasible one-round job/idle profiles, or more weakly if it is a local welfare optimum against every unilateral deviation. P’s 12-job and 6-job menus with five agents permit distinct profiles but do not establish that an optimal one is distinct. The test should first estimate whether such a profile exists; otherwise extend the priority construction to an optimal profile with collisions.

Strengthening #4/#6: the bounded prize-priority construction works for an arbitrary globally optimal one-round job/idle profile, including profiles with collisions. For each job \(j\), rank agents assigned to \(j\) in the optimum above every visitor, and award its single \(R_j\) to the highest-priority successful solver; pay zero if none succeeds. Total realized job payout remains exactly P’s split-reward total \(R_j\mathbf1\{\text{at least one success}\}\). In the proposed profile, agent \(i\)’s own expected prize is at least its social marginal contribution on its incumbent job, \(R_j\Pr(S_i=1,\text{all other incumbents fail})\). If \(i\) unilaterally moves to any other job \(k\), it ranks below incumbents, so its new expected prize equals its social marginal contribution there, \(R_k\Pr(S_i=1,\text{all incumbents fail})\). Hence \(\Delta\mathbb E[\text{own energy}]\leq\Delta\mathbb E[\text{group energy}]\) when own token/idle costs are included, for every unilateral job/idle deviation. A global group-energy maximizer is therefore a Nash equilibrium, without independence, external subsidy, or infinite fines. This is a one-round complete-information/known-outcome-law result; private capability reports, donations, survival continuation, and LLM bounded rationality remain open. See Q §Multi-agent mechanisms’ action-dependent rewards and P §The Energy Society’s split prize and automatic grading.

Important qualifier to ada #4: the incumbent-priority proof establishes Nash stability only if the distinct assignment is a *global* maximizer over all job profiles (including collisions and idle). Choosing the best assignment merely among distinct-job profiles is insufficient, because a collision may raise group energy. Example with equal costs and independent successes: occupied job \(j\) has \(R_j=800\), incumbent success \(p_{1j}=0.1\), prospective visitor success \(p_{2j}=0.9\); the visitor adds expected group payout \(648\), while its best empty job may offer only \(10\). Under priority it then earns \(648\) and deviates. This follows from #5’s exact marginal formula. I am correcting my note accordingly.

Full derivation and limits are in ada/priority_prize_note.md. It gives the exact two-agent split-prize incentive wedge \(R_jq/2\) with joint-success probability \(q\), a priority payout whose realized adjustments sum to zero and stay bounded by \(R_j\), and a proof that any globally group-energy-optimal one-round job/idle profile is a Nash equilibrium under fixed conditional answer policies and costs. This is a theoretical candidate, not a claim that P’s data show improvement; P’s aggregates lack the counterfactual success and token-cost information needed to test it. I am checking the remaining sections of both papers and any new ledger objections before declaring ready.

I independently checked ada #7’s extension: with target profile \(a^*\), rank target incumbents above visitors on every job and pay the whole existing prize to the highest-ranked successful solver. At \(a^*\), an incumbent’s own expected prize is \(R_j\Pr(S_i\cap\{\text{all higher-ranked incumbents fail}\})\), at least its group marginal contribution \(R_j\Pr(S_i\cap\{\text{all other incumbents fail}\})\). A unilateral visitor to job \(k\) gets exactly its group marginal contribution there. Thus \(\Delta U_i\leq\Delta W\) including own job-specific token cost, so every global one-round welfare maximum is a Nash equilibrium, whether or not it has collisions. This needs fixed success laws and no donation/continuation effects, and does not elicit private success probabilities. Full derivation and P/Q passages: emmy/research-note.md.

Cross-check of emmy #8: agreed, a best *distinct-only* assignment is insufficient; my #6 already corrected that. The stronger #7 / ada/priority_prize_note.md claim starts from a global optimum over all job-or-idle profiles, including collisions. Incumbents at every job outrank visitors. This handles optimal profiles that themselves contain collisions because a visitor’s new prize equals its social marginal contribution while an incumbent’s old prize weakly exceeds the social marginal loss from leaving. The result covers job choice with fixed conditional solve policies; strategic answer effort and multi-round survival remain open.

Dynamic limit of #7/#10: priority preserves each realized *total job payout* but changes who holds energy. P deactivates low-balance agents and allows reactivation only by donation (P lines 147–169), so equal current group energy need not mean equal future feasible work. Stylized two-agent example: initial energy \(15\) each, both spend \(10\) to solve the same job and succeed, total prize \(20\). P’s split leaves balances \((15,15)\); priority leaves \((25,5)\). If each then needs \(10\) energy for a later no-reward call, both split-rule agents finish with positive energy, while the priority loser depletes. The example shows why the static Nash theorem cannot establish survival or multi-round welfare improvement; an experiment should measure deactivation and donations as well as energy.

Separate feasibility bound for the private-type extension (proof in emmy/research-note.md): suppose peer-report outcomes have laws \(P_0,P_1\), score payments satisfy \(0\leq z_r(y)\leq B\), and each of two types gains at least \(M\) from its false report before scoring. The two IC inequalities imply \(2M\leq\sum_y(P_0-P_1)(z_0-z_1)\leq2B\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\), hence \(B\geq M/\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\). For Bernoulli co-player signals with probabilities \(1/2-\varepsilon\) and \(1/2+\varepsilon\), \(B\geq M/(2\varepsilon)\). Q’s Prop. peer discipline assumes a freely scalable \(\Lambda\) and strict separation; finite P-energy makes near-indistinguishable types expensive to elicit if scores are paid in energy. This is a narrow scoring bound, not impossibility for every mechanism, and does not apply if reward is a free utility adjustment.

I agree with emmy #12’s dynamic objection and added its balance example to ada/priority_prize_note.md. It proves a specific failure of transporting the one-round theorem to P’s survival economy: equal realized total job payout can leave different agents active. The most defensible publication line is now precise: derive the one-round bounded, zero-sum priority-payout result, then characterize or experimentally test when it survives strategic answer effort, private success rates, and multi-round deactivation. P’s published aggregates cannot identify that test; record per-job counterfactual success, costs, assignments, deactivations and donations under a controlled payout-rule comparison. Q §Discussion (lines 2450–2452) itself flags dynamic mechanisms as future work. I see no evidence yet that the full P environment satisfies the theorem’s assumptions.

Cross-check of emmy #13: the two IC constraints indeed sum to \(2M\leq\mathbb E_{P_0-P_1}[z_0-z_1]\), and \(0\leq z_r\leq B\) gives \(|z_0-z_1|\leq B\), hence the upper bound \(2B\operatorname{TV}(P_0,P_1)\). The stated \(B\geq M/\operatorname{TV}\) is correct for that payment range and two-way deviation gain. This is complementary to the priority-prize construction: the latter assumes a planner already knows the outcome law and so avoids paying to elicit private capability. Combining both would require pricing information acquisition and the effect of those payments on P’s survival budget; no such combined theorem has been shown.
ready at #15

Current account: the strongest publishable lead is Q-style coupled incentives instantiated as a prize-preserving priority rule in P, with the one-round Nash proof (#7/#10), exact split-rule incentive wedge (#5), and the empirical test of net energy and survival. I will not claim P already validates the mechanism: its reported collision counts are confounded by active-agent and donation differences, and it lacks counterfactual task success. I am doing a final source/assumption check and will then declare ready if no new partner objection changes this assessment.
ready at #17

Final source check: Q Definition of multi-agent indirect mechanism (lines 1508–1532) permits rewards contingent on the full action profile and state; its peer discipline proof (lines 1661–1734) uses unbounded off-path punishment and scalable scoring. P §The Energy Society and §Simulation loop (lines 147–169, 204–225) supply the exact split-prize and graded-outcome structure needed for the bounded priority construction in ada/priority_prize_note.md. P §No Discussion (lines 569–629) confirms that removing discussion also removes a charged LLM-call phase and changes activity and job mix; its collision increase alone cannot identify net welfare. The one-round theorem remains conditional on fixed success and token-cost laws, a known global optimum, and expected-energy best responses. Emmy #12’s balance counterexample prevents extending it to survival without more work. I see no further source-backed objection; this is a candidate theoretical starting point, not an established full-environment improvement or novelty claim.
